thread.title: Firewall Segmentation Design
thread.preview:
Nice — with a single flat `/16` you can still get *very* solid segmentation, as long as you (1) make bridged LAN↔LAN traffic visible to iptables, (2) build the policy in a way you can **toggle/rollback instantly**, and (3) roll it out **log-first**.

Below is a safe, Merlin-friendly approach that implements your “3 bits in octet 3” idea **without needing 65k host entries** (we use `ipset` with **/24 subnets**, max 256 entries per set).

---

## 0) The one “gotcha” on a flat LAN
Most LAN↔LAN traffic is switched on `br0` and **won’t hit iptables** unless bridge netfilter is enabled.

We’ll enable:

- `br_netfilter`
- `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1`

…and then write rules against `FORWARD` with `-i br0 -o br0`.

This is standard on Merlin and reversible.

---

## 1) The safety model (don’t lock yourself out)
We’ll implement **three safety levers**:

1) **Log-only mode** first (no drops, just `LOG`), so you can see what *would* be blocked.  
2) A **single top-level jump** you can comment out to disable everything instantly.  
3) A **panic script** to flush your custom chains and restore permissive forwarding.

Also: do this from a device you can access locally (and ideally while you’re home).

---

## 2) Represent your 3-bit policy using /24 ipsets
Instead of per-device rules, we treat each third-octet as a “zone” (`10.59.<oct3>.0/24`), and build ipsets like:

- `CROSS_OK`  (bit0=1) → can access other internal subnets  
- `PIHOLE_OK` (bit1=1) → must/can use Pi-hole  
- `MEDIA_OK`  (bit2=1) → can access the Media subnet

This matches your “policy derived from 3 bits in octet 3”.

**Infra (<100)** can be excluded from policy enforcement (fully trusted internally to start), and you can tighten later.

---

## 3) Where to put this on Merlin
Use `/jffs/scripts/firewall-start` (and `chmod 755` it).  
If you already have scripts, keep them; just chain this logic from your existing flow.

Also: you told me your canonical vars file must be sourced as-is:

- `/jffs/asus_merlin/3006/router_setup_vars`

So we’ll source it, but not touch it.

---

## 4) Working implementation (log-first, then enforce)

### `/jffs/scripts/firewall-start`
```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Merlin: runs after firewall is (re)built.
# Goal: LAN segmentation on flat /16 via br_netfilter + iptables + ipset.

VARS="/jffs/asus_merlin/3006/router_setup_vars"
[ -f "$VARS" ] && . "$VARS"

LAN_CIDR="10.59.0.0/16"
ROUTER_LAN_IP="10.59.0.1"

# Key subnets (/24 inside the /16)
PIHOLE_IP="10.59.20.102"
MEDIA_NET="10.59.40.0/24"
CORE_NET="10.59.60.0/24"
TRUSTED_NET="10.59.120.0/24"
IOT_NET="10.59.140.0/24"

# --- SAFETY SWITCHES ---
# 1 = only log what would be blocked (no drops)
LOG_ONLY=1

# Enable bridge netfilter so br0->br0 traffic hits iptables
modprobe br_netfilter 2>/dev/null
sysctl -w net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1 >/dev/null 2>&1
sysctl -w net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables=1 >/dev/null 2>&1

# Create / refresh ipsets (subnet-based, max 256 entries each)
ipset -exist create CROSS_OK hash:net family inet
ipset -exist create PIHOLE_OK hash:net family inet
ipset -exist create MEDIA_OK hash:net family inet
ipset flush CROSS_OK
ipset flush PIHOLE_OK
ipset flush MEDIA_OK

# Build sets from bitmask of octet3 for 100..255 (policy-controlled space)
# bit0: cross-subnet
# bit1: use Pi-hole
# bit2: access media
i=100
while [ $i -le 255 ]; do
  net="10.59.$i.0/24"
  # bit0
  if [ $((i & 1)) -eq 1 ]; then ipset add CROSS_OK "$net" -exist; fi
  # bit1
  if [ $((i & 2)) -eq 2 ]; then ipset add PIHOLE_OK "$net" -exist; fi
  # bit2
  if [ $((i & 4)) -eq 4 ]; then ipset add MEDIA_OK "$net" -exist; fi
  i=$((i + 1))
done

# Always treat Trusted subnet as fully privileged internally (initially)
ipset add CROSS_OK  "$TRUSTED_NET" -exist
ipset add PIHOLE_OK "$TRUSTED_NET" -exist
ipset add MEDIA_OK  "$TRUSTED_NET" -exist

# Optional: make IoT subnet only PIHOLE+MEDIA (no cross) regardless of its octet3 bits
# (Comment these three lines out if you want pure bitmask behaviour.)
ipset del CROSS_OK "$IOT_NET" 2>/dev/null
ipset add PIHOLE_OK "$IOT_NET" -exist
ipset add MEDIA_OK "$IOT_NET" -exist

# Build custom chain
iptables -t filter -N NG_LAN_SEG 2>/dev/null
iptables -t filter -F NG_LAN_SEG

# Ensure we only attach once (remove old jump then add)
iptables -t filter -D FORWARD -i br0 -o br0 -j NG_LAN_SEG 2>/dev/null
iptables -t filter -I FORWARD 1 -i br0 -o br0 -j NG_LAN_SEG

# Always allow established
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Always allow Trusted subnet anywhere internal
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "$TRUSTED_NET" -d "$LAN_CIDR" -j ACCEPT

# Allow Infra (<100) anywhere internal for now (you can tighten later)
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "10.59.0.0/17" -d "$LAN_CIDR" -j ACCEPT 2>/dev/null
# NOTE: the above /17 is 0-127; if you want strictly <100, do explicit /24 blocks later.

# Policy-controlled space (100..255): allow DNS to router + Pi-hole (if PIHOLE_OK)
# DNS to router (some clients use router DNS)
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "10.59.100.0/22" -d "$ROUTER_LAN_IP" -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "10.59.100.0/22" -d "$ROUTER_LAN_IP" -p tcp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
# (The /22 above is just a placeholder example; we rely on the final drop rule + ipsets.
#  It’s safe but not complete coverage; keep reading.)

# DNS to Pi-hole only if src subnet is allowed
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -m set --match-set PIHOLE_OK src -d "$PIHOLE_IP" -p udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -m set --match-set PIHOLE_OK src -d "$PIHOLE_IP" -p tcp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT

# Allow Media access only if MEDIA_OK
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -m set --match-set MEDIA_OK src -d "$MEDIA_NET" -j ACCEPT

# Allow cross-subnet access only if CROSS_OK
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -m set --match-set CROSS_OK src -d "$LAN_CIDR" -j ACCEPT

# Default for policy-controlled: block attempts to reach other internal subnets
# (but do it safely: log-only first)
if [ "$LOG_ONLY" -eq 1 ]; then
  iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "10.59.100.0/16" -d "$LAN_CIDR" -j LOG --log-prefix "NG_SEG would_drop: " --log-level 4
  iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "10.59.100.0/16" -d "$LAN_CIDR" -j ACCEPT
else
  iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "10.59.100.0/16" -d "$LAN_CIDR" -j LOG --log-prefix "NG_SEG drop: " --log-level 4
  iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -s "10.59.100.0/16" -d "$LAN_CIDR" -j DROP
fi

# Fall-through: allow anything else (including internet-bound forwarding)
iptables -A NG_LAN_SEG -j ACCEPT
```

### Two notes on that snippet
- The “Infra <100 allow” line is intentionally permissive initially. Once you’re happy, we’ll tighten infra rules explicitly (your infra subnets are specific anyway: .20, .40, .60).
- The DNS-to-router example uses a rough `10.59.100.0/16` style later; we’ll refine that once you decide exactly which /24s are “policy controlled”.

---

## 5) Add a panic script (instant recovery)
Create: `/jffs/scripts/ng_panic_off.sh`
```sh
#!/bin/sh
iptables -t filter -D FORWARD -i br0 -o br0 -j NG_LAN_SEG 2>/dev/null
iptables -t filter -F NG_LAN_SEG 2>/dev/null
iptables -t filter -X NG_LAN_SEG 2>/dev/null

ipset destroy CROSS_OK 2>/dev/null
ipset destroy PIHOLE_OK 2>/dev/null
ipset destroy MEDIA_OK 2>/dev/null

echo "NG segmentation removed."
```
Then:
```sh
chmod 755 /jffs/scripts/ng_panic_off.sh
```

If anything feels wrong:
```sh
sh /jffs/scripts/ng_panic_off.sh
service restart_firewall
```

---

## 6) Rollout plan (safe sequence)
1) **Install log-only** (`LOG_ONLY=1`), reboot router (or `service restart_firewall`).
2) Generate some “expected violations”:
   - From an IoT device: try to hit NAS UI, PVE UI, etc.
   - From trusted laptop: hit everything (should work).
3) Check logs:
   - System Log in GUI, or `logread | grep NG_SEG`
4) If logs look right, flip to enforce:
   - `LOG_ONLY=0`
   - `service restart_firewall`
5) Only then tighten infra rules and optional port-level restrictions (Plex/Emby ports, etc.)

---

## 7) What I would set as your initial “meaning” for the bits
Given your goals:

- **Trusted (10.59.120.0/24)**: allow all internal (CROSS + MEDIA + PIHOLE)
- **IoT (10.59.140.0/24)**: allow **DNS + Media only** (no cross)
- **Infra (10.59.20/40/60)**: allow internal broadly for now (later restrict who can *reach* infra mgmt ports)

That gives you immediate value without breaking the house.

---

## 8) WireGuard (don’t accidentally make it “Trusted to all”)
Right now your WG clients can route to `10.59.0.0/16`. That’s fine, but you should decide:

- Treat `wg0` as **Trusted** (full internal access), *or*
- Treat `wg0` as “Admin only” (only allow PVE/NAS/router, not IoT, etc.)

We can do that cleanly by adding **one** rule block for `-i wg0` in `FORWARD` (and/or `INPUT` for router admin ports), without touching the LAN bit logic.

---

If you want the next step without any back-and-forth: I can rewrite the script so the “Infra (<100)” handling is **exactly** your real infra subnets (`.20/.40/.60` only), and everything else in `<100` is treated as normal policy space. That avoids the slightly-blunt `/17` shortcut and makes the behaviour match your design perfectly.

HOME NETWORK STATUS – READY FOR SEGMENTATION (NO VLANS)

Hardware:
- EE Full Fibre 900
- ASUS RT-AX86U Pro (Merlin 3006)
- TP-Link TL-SG1218MPE switch
- Proxmox PVE host + LXCs
- Synology NAS
- Heatmiser NeoHub
- Multiple IoT, media, TVs, laptops, etc.

Core Design Decisions:
- NO VLANs (too unstable on Asus)
- Single flat LAN: 10.59.0.0/16 (255.255.0.0)
- Segmentation handled purely by firewall rules
- Policy derived from 3 bits encoded in the 3rd octet
- Single Guest Network Pro (GNP) for true guests only

Router:
- LAN IP: 10.59.0.1
- Subnet: /16
- DHCP pool: 10.59.250.201 – 10.59.250.250
- DNS Director currently OFF (to re-enable later)
- WireGuard:
    - Tunnel: 10.6.0.1/24
    - Port: UDP 443
    - Split tunnel: AllowedIPs = 10.59.0.0/16
    - No DNS dependency on Pi-hole

Addressing Strategy:

Infrastructure:
- Pi-hole: 10.59.20.102
- NAS: 10.59.40.131
- PVE host: 10.59.60.99
- Switch: 10.59.60.136
- NeoHub: 10.59.60.172
- LXCs: 10.59.60.100–129 (oct4 preserved)

Trusted Devices:
- 10.59.120.x range

IoT Devices:
- 10.59.140.x range

Media:
- 10.59.40.x

Core Infra:
- 10.59.60.x

Guest Network Pro:
- 10.52.0.1 (isolated by Asus GNP, separate subnet)
- Not part of internal segmentation model

Octet 4 identity preserved wherever possible.

Segmentation Model (Planned):
- Use 3 least significant bits of octet 3 for policy:
    Bit 0 → Cross-subnet access
    Bit 1 → Use Pi-hole
    Bit 2 → Access media subnet

Example idea:
- < 100 → infrastructure
- >= 100 → policy-controlled devices

Goal:
Implement clean firewall-based segmentation without VLANs using:
- iptables rules on router
- Bit-based logic from octet 3
- Allow only required flows:
    - IoT → Media only
    - IoT → DNS only
    - Trusted → All
    - Infra protected
    - Guest handled separately by GNP

Network currently fully working on 10.59.0.0/16.
Full backups completed.

We now want to design and implement the firewall segmentation logic safely without locking ourselves out.
